text: Τὸ μηδὲν ὄντι τὸ σύνολον. Nihil prorsus dicit numerum, quod supra res numerata nihil verae entitatis addat, sed pro earum ratione, vel in rerum natura, vel in sola mente concipiente existat; ab illa denique utroque-modo complementum habeat. Formalitates vocant, seu entia metaphysica, ac conceptas rationes: quibus physicos effectus, qualis divisio est, tribuere, merito Maximus absurdum habet.
anchorLine: ὁ μηδὲν ὄντι τὸ σύνολον (f), οὐκ οὐσία, οὐ ποιὸν,
en: The phrase Τὸ μηδὲν ὄντι τὸ σύνολον. He says that number adds nothing of true entity over and above the things numbered, but exists, according to their nature, either in the nature of things or only in the mind that conceives it; and from the latter, in either way, it has its completion. They call these formalities, that is, metaphysical entities and conceived notions; and to ascribe to them physical effects, such as division is, Maximus rightly holds absurd.

text: Πᾶσαν θείαν καὶ ἀνθρωπίνην. Sic Mono-[the]litæ utrinque sibi cavere videbantur scopulum, [ut supra] n. 8, dictum est; ut neque cum Severo aliisque [su]perioribus confunderent, nec cum Nestorio ipsis-[qu]e Catholicis (in cujus partes eos male arcesse-[ba]nt) dividerent. Quin ipse quoque Joannes Con-[s]tantinopolitanus ejusque synodus, Bardano impe-[rat]ore, fucum se illis fecisse arbitrati sunt, ac [ca]tholicam fidem confessos esse, ipsis his eorum [ver]bis, et ad eam confitendam, imprudentem ipsum [ad p]ravum induxisse; suppressa duntaxat voce unius [et] duarum, quæ videretur in Ecclesiis turbas [move]re: quidquid sit de hac illorum dispensatione [Joan]nis scilicet et sociorum episcoporum, in qui-[bus] etiam fuere viri sanctitate conspicui), num reipsa proditæ fidei damnandi sint, Baroniana cen-sura, aut certe mitius habendi, vel etiam pro dispensationis solertia laudandi, qua ab Ecclesiis tantum depulerint turbinem, quantum per hæretici principis tyrannidem cernebant illis ingruere. Pu-tem Constantinum papam eorum accepisse satisfa-ctionem, nec austerius in ipsos quæsiisse, quos agnosceret catholicam reipsa animo fidem tenuisse, nec quidquam magis quam Ecclesiarum incolumi-tatem in eo negotio spectasse. Ipse Maximus sanum hic sensum deprehendit, si eumdem ipsum Christum secundum aliud et aliud, quod vere erat, alia atque alia, exque ipsorum ratione, pro communis personæ ac compositæ munere, intelligamus operatum esse; quod tamen negat Monothelitas voluisse. Certe si
anchorLine: πλίας, τῷ λέγειν, Πᾶσαν θείαν καὶ ἀνθρωπίνην (m)

en: Πᾶσαν θείαν καὶ ἀνθρωπίνην. Thus the Monothelites seemed to guard themselves against a reef on both sides, as was said above (n. 8): so as neither to be confused with Severus and the others before him, nor to be divided from Nestorius and the Catholics themselves (towards whom they were wrongly pushed). Indeed John of Constantinople himself and his synod, under the emperor Bardanes, thought they had made fools of them [the Monothelites], and that these had confessed the Catholic faith in the very words of their own party, and that they had led the imprudent man [the emperor] to confess it, with only the phrase 'of one and of two' (which seemed to cause disturbances in the Churches) suppressed. Whatever may be said of this dispensation of John and his fellow bishops (among whom were also men conspicuous for holiness), whether they are to be condemned as having in fact betrayed the faith, as the Baronian censure would have it, or at least judged more mildly, or even praised for the skill of their dispensation, by which they warded off from the Churches as great a storm as they saw threatening them from the tyranny of a heretical prince; I think Pope Constantine accepted their satisfaction and did not press them more severely, since he recognised that they in fact held the catholic faith in their minds and had regarded nothing more in that business than the safety of the Churches. Maximus himself finds a sound sense here if we understand that the same Christ himself operated according to one and another [nature], that is, according to what he truly was, by different [operations], and from their [the natures'] account, in the capacity of a common and composite person; which, however, the Monothelites deny they intended. Surely if...

text: Ὅροι ἑνώσεων. Brevem hunc tractatum, postremum pene habet Turrianus, etsi non integrum, Græca, Romanus codex superioribus subjiciebat. Quam 1 ponit, unitio est, ἡ κατ᾽ οὐσίαν· quam debemus accipere ut distinctam contra sequentem, quæ est, ἡ καθ᾽ ὑπόστασιν· quarum etiam magis conditiones exponit in fine; quod, ἡ κατ᾽ οὐσίαν, sit in diversis hypostasibus, seu personis et individuis; ἡ καθ᾽ ὑπόστασιν vero, in diversis substantiis seu naturis. Cyrillus tamen et Patres alii, οὐσιώδη et φυσικὴν ipsam unionem in Christo ὑποστατικὴν vocitant, quasi veram, et ut distinguant contra σχετικὴν Nestorii, id est, affectu solo constantem, qualis est in sanctis per gratiam. Hypostasibus individuorum, non satis apte Turr. quod Maximus, ἐπὶ τῶν ὑποστάσεων, τουτέστιν ἀτόμων, nisi aliter ejus codex habuerit, ac certe aliter habuisse putem, nempe, ἐπὶ τῶν ὑποστάσεων, τῶν ἀτόμων, quæ sic ille sibi redenda putaverit, cum esset reddendum: In hypostasibus, quæ sunt individua; qui modus loquendi Græcis familiarissimus, ac in illis Maximo. In seq. habuisse videtur, ὡς ἐπὶ ψυχῆς καὶ σώματος, quod et clarius est, ac libens sequor.
anchorLine: Ὅροι ἑνώσεων (n).
unreadable: Gutter edge clips the opening letters of many left-column lines (e.g. 'ἐπὶ', 'ὁσιώδη', 'ejus', 'nempe', 'ille', 'loquendi'); letters read from context ('οὐσιώδη', 'ὑποστατικὴν', 'ἐπὶ', 'ejus', 'ille', 'loquendi') are the visible part restored by the word, and the Greek 'quæ sic ille sibi redenda' is printed 'redenda'. A marginal '1' stands in 'Quam 1 ponit' as printed.
en: Ὅροι ἑνώσεων (Definitions of unions). Turrianus has this short treatise almost last, though not complete; the Greek the Roman codex appended to the above. The union which he places first is that κατ᾽ οὐσίαν, which we must take as distinct from the one following, which is ἡ καθ᾽ ὑπόστασιν; and he sets out the conditions of both more fully at the end: namely, that the union according to essence is in diverse hypostases, that is persons and individuals, while that according to hypostasis is in diverse substances or natures. Cyril and other Fathers, however, call the union in Christ itself essential and natural, and hypostatic, as being true, and to distinguish it from the relational union of Nestorius, that is, one standing in affection alone, such as is in the saints by grace. 'Hypostases of individuals': Turrianus renders this not very aptly, in that Maximus [says] ἐπὶ τῶν ὑποστάσεων, that is, of individuals, unless his codex read otherwise, and I think it certainly read otherwise, namely ἐπὶ τῶν ὑποστάσεων, τῶν ἀτόμων, which he thought he should render as it ought to have been rendered: In hypostases, which are individuals; a mode of speaking very familiar to the Greeks, and to Maximus among them. In what follows he seems to have had ὡς ἐπὶ ψυχῆς καὶ σώματος (as in soul and body), which is also clearer, and I gladly follow it.

text: Ἡ κατὰ σχέσιν. Turr. secundum habitudinem reddit; sequentia non reddens, ὡς ἐπὶ τῶν γνωμῶν· quæ facile erat illi reddere, et ex illis vim τοῦ κατὰ σχέσιν, ex Maximi mente, et theologorum adversus Nestorium, magis perdiscere seu explicare. Est ergo unitio quæ est per affectum, libera voluntate et ex arbitrio, cum plures per concordiam una sententia, unus animus, una voluntas sunt: Εἷς ἓν θέλημα, ut sit una voluntas, non quod reddit idem Turr. ut una voluntatibus. Hæc nempe una Christi voluntas Nestorio, ejusque ταυτοβουλίας (consensu scilicet in objecto) quæ communis est sanctorum cum Deo, a quorum communi classe ἀνθρωπολάτρης hæreticus Christum non eximebat: nullam substantialem unitionem, ac vere subsistendi ratione, in eo ponens, sed solam affectualem (ut sic loquar) et quæ est per gratiam, in qua solum haberet potiores partes, ut qui reliquis, acceptis a Deo melius usus esset, exque profectu, in Filium Dei evasisset, non a prima exsistentia, natura Filius exstitisset. Hæc sic impura ac Judaica Nestorii, in quem nemo Catholicorum indulgentior esse debeat, et ut malum potius metaphysicum quam scelestissime in Filium Dei blasphemum, ejusque omne dispensationis evertentem mysterium, ingerat. Qui de hara Calvini Ministellus Septimania tentavit haud ita pridem Nestorium levare, Cyrillo detrahere, is suas in se contineat tenebras, nec orci novam fuliginem (cui satis sit Calvinianus candor hactenus Christianissimo orbe tantum non repressus) in claram ejus pubem, celebri orbis Lycæo procul aspergat.
anchorLine: Ἡ κατὰ σχέσιν (o) ἕνωσις, ἐπὶ τῶν γνωμῶν, εἰς ἓν θέλημα.
unreadable: Gutter clipping at the left of left-column lines and at the right of right-column lines. Printed as read: 'redenda', 'Ministellus', 'Septimania' (single words as printed); the first letters of several left-column lines are cut. The words 'ut una voluntatibus' (printed 'ut una voluntatibus' after 'Turr.') and 'metaphysicum' were read in a damaged print; ':' after 'sunt' as printed. The right-column lines run on the page's gutter edge so some endings ('exque', 'impura', 'evertentem', 'continea…', 'celeb…') may lack a last letter.
en: Ἡ κατὰ σχέσιν (the union by relation). Turrianus renders it 'according to habit', not rendering what follows, ὡς ἐπὶ τῶν γνωμῶν (as in the case of judgements); which it was easy for him to render, and from these to learn more thoroughly the force of κατὰ σχέσιν, according to Maximus's mind and that of the theologians against Nestorius. So it is a union that is through affection, by free will and choice, when many through agreement are of one mind, one purpose, one will: Εἷς ἓν θέλημα, 'that there be one will', not as Turrianus renders it, 'that there be one in wills'. This one will of Christ, then, [belonged] to Nestorius, and his ταυτοβουλία (agreement of will in the object) which is common to the saints with God; from whose common class the man-worshipping heretic did not exempt Christ, placing in him no substantial union and none by true subsistence, but only an affective one (so to speak), which is through grace, in which he would only have the better parts, so that as one who had made better use of what he had received from God, and from progress, he came to be the Son of God, and was not Son by nature from the first existence. This impure and Jewish doctrine of Nestorius, against whom no Catholic should be too indulgent, also imports a metaphysical evil rather than the most wicked blasphemy against the Son of God, one overturning the whole mystery of the dispensation. Let him who of late, from the Calvinist brood, the little minister of Septimania, attempted to lighten Nestorius and to disparage Cyril, keep his own darkness within himself, and not sprinkle a new soot of hell (for whom the Calvinist candour hitherto, scarcely restrained by the most Christian world, should suffice) upon the famous bright face of the learned world's Lyceum.

text: Ἡ καθ᾽ ἁρμονίαν. Idem atque ἁρμός, commissura, compago. In animalibus proprie dicitur; hincque adeo in ædificiis, quorum structura sic maxime alii aliis lapides committuntur. Ἁρμὸς λίθου, Lapidis commissura, citatur ex Schol. Aristophanis.
anchorLine: Ἡ κατὰ ἁρμονίαν (p) ἕνωσις, ἐπὶ τῶν λίθων.
unreadable: First letters of the lines are clipped at the gutter; the key phrase 'sic maxime' is read from the damaged line ending '…ime' and may be a little off.
en: Ἡ καθ᾽ ἁρμονίαν (the union by fitting). The same as ἁρμός, a joint, a fastening. It is properly said of animals, and hence also of buildings, whose structure is such that stones are joined most closely to one another. Ἁρμὸς λίθου, 'a joint of stone', is cited from the scholiast on Aristophanes.

en: Ἡ κατὰ συναλοιφήν (the union by anointing together). He explains most acutely this union, which is of the greatest account to Greek theologians.

text: Maximus ex eorum mente. Nempe advertit vir divinus in theologia maxime usurpari hanc unitionem, et ab illa, uno omnium Patrum consensu removeri: ita nimirum ut veras in Deo intelligamus emanationes, quibus reipsa personæ procedant, Filius et Spiritus, qui tamen cum Patre auctore non coalescant ac confundantur, sive etiam inter se, sed suam quæque hypostasim, et quod vere in persona exsistunt, habeant. Næ igitur frigide Turr. unio secundum conjunctionem. Certe quæ secundum conjunctionem unitio est, haud ita abhorret a Trinitate. Nam quæ major conjunctio, quam qua una persona in altera est, et quasi illi immeat, per συμπεριχώρησιν, quam theologi Græci vocant. Est ergo conjunctio (non enim divisio et separatio), sed sine confusione, veraque eorum quæ sic conjuncta sunt, distinctione. Greg. orat. De theol. ἐνοῦμεν δὲ τὴν θεότητα, καὶ οὐκ εἰς ἓν τὰ τρία συναλείφομεν. Chrysost. in I ad Cor. Οὐ τὰς ὑποστάσεις συναλείφων, ἀλλὰ τῆς οὐσίας τὴν ὁμοτιμίαν ἐμφαίνων. Damasc. De Trin. Ἑνοῦνται γὰρ αἱ ὑποστάσεις, καὶ τὴν ἐν ἀλλήλαις περιχώρησιν ἔχουσι, δίχα πάσης συναλοιφῆς καὶ συμφύρσεως. Reddat Turr. Uniuntur et inter se commeant absque ulla conjunctione. Ergo summo divortio. Implicat certe in adjecto. Mihi, absque ulla coalitione, concretione et quasi conflato, et confusione. Συναλείφειν Gregorio, τὸ συναιρεῖν· et συναλοιφή, συναίρεσις, Sabelli propria; conjunctio quasi elisione, et quasi ad unum medium redactis quæ uniuntur, extremisque compressis, velut fere apud grammaticos fit in syllabis. More nostro loquimur in divinis, in quibus tamen non licet communibus Patrumque vocibus resilire, vel ita detorquere. Hæc satis pro opusculi parvitate.
anchorLine: (anchor is the (q) call on p-0125: Ἡ κατὰ συναλοιφήν (q) ἕνωσις)
unreadable: Continuation of note (q) from p-0125, no marker repeated. The gutter-edge letters of the left column lines are partly clipped; the Chrysostom quotation lines 'συναλεί-|[φ]ων' and 'ἐμφαίνων' are damaged in the scan: the line is read '…ων. ἀλλὰ τῆς οὐσίας τὴν ὁμοτιμίαν ἐμφαίνων' with the first letters illegible, 'συναλείφων' restored from the hyphenated 'συναλεί-' and the surviving 'ων', and should be verified; 'συναίρεσις' is printed 'συναίρεσις' with a blurred second letter; 'συμπεριχώρησιν' is partly dotted in the print.
en: Maximus, from their mind. The divine man notes that this 'union' is chiefly used in theology, and is by the one consent of all the Fathers removed from it: so that we understand true emanations in God, by which the persons actually proceed, the Son and the Spirit, who however with the Father as source do not grow together and are not confounded, or even among themselves, but each has its own hypostasis, and what truly exists in a person. So Turrianus is flat in [rendering] 'union according to conjunction'. Surely a union that is according to conjunction does not so much shrink from the Trinity. For what greater conjunction than that by which one person is in another and as it were dwells in him, through περιχώρησις, as the Greek theologians call it. There is therefore a conjunction (for it is not division and separation), but without confusion, and with a true distinction of what is thus conjoined. Gregory, orat. De theol.: ἐνοῦμεν δὲ τὴν θεότητα, καὶ οὐκ εἰς ἓν τὰ τρία συναλείφομεν. Chrysostom on 1 Cor.: Οὐ τὰς ὑποστάσεις συναλείφων, ἀλλὰ τῆς οὐσίας τὴν ὁμοτιμίαν ἐμφαίνων. Damascene, De Trin.: Ἑνοῦνται γὰρ αἱ ὑποστάσεις, καὶ τὴν ἐν ἀλλήλαις περιχώρησιν ἔχουσι, δίχα πάσης συναλοιφῆς καὶ συμφύρσεως. Let Turrianus render: 'They are united and dwell in one another without any conjunction.' Therefore [it is] at the greatest distance. It certainly implies a contradiction in the added term. To me, 'without any coalition, concretion and as it were fusion, and confusion.' Συναλείφειν in Gregory is τὸ συναιρεῖν (to contract); and συναλοιφή, συναίρεσις is proper to Sabellius; a conjunction as if by elision, with the things united brought to one middle and their extremes squeezed together, as it nearly happens in syllables among grammarians. We speak in our usual way in things divine, in which however it is not lawful to recoil from the common words of the Fathers, nor so to distort them. This is enough for the smallness of the opusculum.

text: Καὶ συνοδικαρίου. Sit forte qui judiciis ecclesiasticis præerat, vel qui ab epistolis quasi synodalibus Paulo archiepiscopo esset. Num quasi ἔκδικος seu συνέκδικος, defensor, vindex? Quid si ambæ jungendæ voces, Ῥήτορος καὶ συνοδικαρίου, ut altera alteram exponat, sitque orator, cujus partium erat ut pontificias sanctiones ac decreta exponeret? seu etiam ex illorum ratione subditis jus diceret; qualis fere quem episcopi officialem vocant. Vellem certiora monumenta, quibus ejus munus totum explicari posset. Valde certe infelicitus homo, qui nugas ejusmodi, magis quam subtile aliquid habentes quæstiones, obtruderet.

en: Καὶ συνοδικαρίου ('and synodical official'). Perhaps he who presided over ecclesiastical courts, or who was in charge of what we might call synodal letters under Paul the archbishop. Is he as it were an ἔκδικος or συνέκδικος, a defender, an avenger? What if the two words are to be joined, Ῥήτορος καὶ συνοδικαρίου, so that one explains the other, and he be an orator whose part it was to expound pontifical sanctions and decrees? or also, according to their reckoning, to dispense justice to subjects, such as the person whom bishops call an official. I would like surer records by which his whole function might be explained. A very unhappy man indeed, to press such trifles, which hold questions rather than anything subtle.

text: Τὰ τῆς ἀγνωμοσύνης ῥήματα. Nempe Eunomii, qui a Christo ac de Christo dicta ad ejus astruendam humanitatem, ac quibus ipsius in humanum genus commendetur dignatio ac benignitas, in illius deitatis injuriam improbe summaque ingratitudine trahebat, uti etiam Billius observavit. Chrysostomo passim εὐγνωμοσύνης verba, relata scilicet ad Christum, qui illa verborum expressione Patri deferat, et se illi minime contrarium ostendat, suamque cum originem agnoscat.
anchorLine: τῆς ἀγνωμοσύνης ῥήματα (s), τὸ, Θεός μου, καὶ
unreadable: Gutter edge clips the first letters of the left-column lines 2-4; last word of line 4 of the right-hand part is a smudge ('ostendat' read as 'ostenda…'); 'Ἁγνωμοσύνης' in the printed lemma is distorted ('ἀγνωμοσύνης' read from the Greek text of the same word).
en: Τὰ τῆς ἀγνωμοσύνης ῥήματα (the words of ingratitude). Namely, of Eunomius, who dragged the things said by Christ and about Christ, to establish his humanity, and by which his condescension and kindness toward mankind are commended, wickedly and with the greatest ingratitude into an insult to his deity, as Billius also observed. In Chrysostom the words of gratitude (εὐγνωμοσύνης) occur everywhere, referred to Christ, who by that expression of words defers to the Father, shows himself not at all contrary to him, and acknowledges his own origin.

text: Οἰκείωσις δέ. Scite Maximus arrogationem distinguit, qua sibi quis arrogat, quæ reipsa habet, et qua ea, quæ sunt aliorum, ut se unum quid cum illis reputat. Sic in Christo præter naturalia, ipsa vere et in unitione, in ipso exsistentia, κατ᾽ οἰκείωσιν proinde naturalem, ut idem Maximus loquitur; quæ sibi vere ac natura Christus vindicaret ac tribueret; erant ἐν τῇ κατ᾽ ἐπίνοιαν διαστολῇ, ut subtili mentis cogitatu a deitate quasi sejuncta caro intelligebatur, ac unum nobiscum ratione hominis, velut præcisione a Verbo sustentante, atque eam habente; κατ᾽ οἰκείωσιν σχετικήν, arrogatione illa quæ est secundum affectum, ac quadam necessitudine, etiam illa quæ nobis ex peccato inoleverunt; ignorantia, non subjectio, et similia: ipsa vere nunquam in ipso, quod neque in illa præcisione, sed vere semper in unitione: at neque in nobis ut συστατικά, quasi ad naturam pertinentia, illamque constituentia, sed pravæ voluntatis labe invecta. Idem clarius sequenti ad Marinum tomo dogmatico.
anchorLine: τῆς ἀγνωμοσύνης ῥήματα (s) [call on p-0127]; this (t) call is at 'Οἰκείωσιν δὲ (t), ποίαν ἄρα φασί;' in the Greek column of p-0128
unreadable: Gutter-edge clipping of the first letters of several left-column lines (e.g. 'astruendam', 'in illius' style clipping is on p-0127 not here); here the right column of the note is complete. The anchorWord/Line is not located at 600 dpi (the (t) call in the Greek column was not cut separately); anchor given from the note's own lemma Οἰκείωσιν δέ.
en: Οἰκείωσις δέ (appropriation). Maximus rightly distinguishes arrogation, by which one claims for oneself what one really has, and that by which one counts what belongs to others as one thing with oneself. So in Christ, besides the natural things, the very ones truly in him and in the union, existing in him, according to appropriation, hence natural, as Maximus himself says, which Christ would claim and attribute to himself truly and by nature; they were in the division κατ᾽ ἐπίνοιαν (by thought), as the flesh was understood by the subtle thought of the mind as sundered from the deity, and one with us in the account of man, as by a precision from the sustaining Word who has it; κατ᾽ οἰκείωσιν σχετικήν (by relational appropriation), by that arrogation which is according to affection and a certain necessity, even those things which have grown in us from sin: ignorance, not subjection, and the like: these are never truly in him, since neither in that precision but truly always in the union; but neither in us as constitutive, as if belonging to nature and constituting it, but as brought in by the stain of a depraved will. The same more clearly in the following dogmatic tome to Marinus.

text: Κατάγνωσις φύσεως. Nempe velle mori, quasi naturæ abdicatio est ac damnatio; cum ipsa esse et vivere appetat. Nec qui altiori proposito mortem contemnunt, ipsi mortem ambiunt, aut vitam defugiunt, sed meliorem vitam deteriori præferunt.
anchorLine: γνωσις φύσεώς (u) ἐστι γὰρ τοῦτο. Καὶ πῶς ἂν φησι
unreadable: Print is smudged at the left edge ('esse et vivere' read 'esic ot'; 'cum ipsa' with a blurred 'i'); read from context. 'meliorem' printed 'incliorem' by the type, read as meliorem.
en: Κατάγνωσις φύσεως (condemnation of nature). Namely, to wish to die is as it were a renunciation and condemnation of nature, since nature itself desires to be and to live. Nor do those who, for a higher purpose, despise death themselves seek death, or flee life, but prefer a better life to a worse one.
